questions.text: How is total cost decomposed in the short run?

options.a: Marginal cost plus average cost.
options.b: Variable cost plus fixed cost.
options.c: Revenue minus profit plus consumer surplus.
options.d: Producer surplus plus utility.

questions.text: How is average cost defined for positive output y?

options.a: Fixed cost divided by marginal cost.
options.b: Revenue divided by output.
options.c: Marginal cost times output.
options.d: Total cost divided by output.

questions.text: What is average variable cost?

options.a: Total cost divided by price.
options.b: Total revenue minus variable cost.
options.c: Variable cost divided by output.
options.d: Fixed cost divided by output.

questions.text: What is average fixed cost?

options.a: Price multiplied by output.
options.b: Variable cost divided by output.
options.c: Fixed cost divided by output.
options.d: Marginal cost minus average cost.

questions.text: What is the accounting relationship among AC, AVC and AFC?

options.a: AC = AVC + AFC.
options.b: AC = MC + total revenue.
options.c: AC = AVC - AFC.
options.d: AC = AVC times AFC.

questions.text: As output expands with positive fixed cost, what happens to average fixed cost?

options.a: It remains constant.
options.b: It becomes negative.
options.c: It rises linearly.
options.d: It falls.

questions.text: Why can an average total cost curve be U-shaped?

options.a: Fixed cost rises at exactly the same rate as output.
options.b: All cost components are always increasing.
options.c: Falling average fixed cost can initially dominate, while rising average variable cost can dominate later.
options.d: Marginal cost is necessarily negative initially.

questions.text: What does a vertical gap between AC and AVC measure at a particular output?

options.a: Marginal revenue.
options.b: Average fixed cost.
options.c: The product price.
options.d: Total fixed cost regardless of output.

questions.text: What is marginal cost?

options.a: The average cost of a unit already produced.
options.b: The rate at which minimum total cost changes as output increases.
options.c: The opportunity cost of buying a product as a consumer.
options.d: The total cost of producing all output.

questions.text: Why does fixed cost not enter short-run marginal cost when it does not vary with output?

options.a: Its derivative with respect to output is zero.
options.b: Fixed cost is always negative.
options.c: Fixed cost is included in marginal revenue.
options.d: Variable cost cannot affect marginal cost.

questions.text: If marginal cost is below average variable cost, what is happening to AVC as output increases locally?

options.a: AVC is falling.
options.b: AVC is necessarily constant.
options.c: Total variable cost is falling.
options.d: AVC is rising.

questions.text: If marginal cost is above average variable cost, what is happening to AVC locally?

options.a: AVC is rising.
options.b: Fixed cost must be negative.
options.c: AVC is falling.
options.d: AVC must be zero.

questions.text: At an interior minimum of a smooth AVC curve, what relation holds?

options.a: MC = AFC.
options.b: AC = 0.
options.c: MC = AVC.
options.d: MC = AC + AVC.

questions.text: At an interior minimum of a smooth AC curve, what relation holds?

options.a: MC = 0.
options.b: MC = AC.
options.c: MC is less than AC.
options.d: MC = AVC at every output.

questions.text: If MC is below AC, what happens to average total cost as output increases?

options.a: It declines locally.
options.b: It remains exactly constant by definition.
options.c: It increases locally.
options.d: It immediately equals zero.

questions.text: If MC is above AC, what happens to average total cost as output increases?

options.a: It cannot be defined.
options.b: It is necessarily negative.
options.c: It rises locally.
options.d: It falls locally.

questions.text: What is the intuition behind MC crossing AC at its minimum?

options.a: A marginal unit cheaper than the current average pulls the average down; a dearer marginal unit pulls it up.
options.b: Marginal cost always grows faster than total cost.
options.c: Average cost depends only on marginal revenue.
options.d: Every marginal unit must equal fixed cost.

questions.text: If average fixed cost is positive, how do AC and AVC compare at a given output?

options.a: AC is below AVC.
options.b: AC exceeds AVC.
options.c: No relationship is possible.
options.d: AC equals AVC for every output.

questions.text: What is the relationship between variable cost and the marginal cost curve for continuously variable output?

options.a: Variable cost equals fixed cost plus average cost.
options.b: Variable cost equals marginal cost at the last unit only.
options.c: Variable cost equals the area above the price line.
options.d: Variable cost from zero to y is the area under MC over that range when variable cost at zero is zero.

questions.text: For a good produced in discrete units, how can variable cost be expressed?

options.a: Subtract total revenue from all fixed costs.
options.b: Sum the average fixed costs of each unit.
options.c: Sum the marginal costs of units 1 through y, when variable cost at zero is zero.
options.d: Multiply the marginal cost of unit y by y irrespective of earlier units.

questions.text: Why does integrating marginal cost recover total variable cost, but not an unrelated fixed cost?

options.a: Integrating always yields revenue.
options.b: Marginal cost and average cost are identical.
options.c: Marginal cost is the derivative of variable cost; a fixed component has zero derivative.
options.d: Fixed cost has a negative derivative.

questions.text: If total cost is c(y)=F+3y+y^2, what is marginal cost?
If variable cost is zero at zero output, what is the definite integral of MC from 0 to y?

options.a: AC(y).
options.b: cv(y).
options.c: F.
options.d: p times y.

questions.text: For a firm producing the same product in two plants, what is the efficient allocation of output at an interior optimum?

options.a: Equalize average total costs across plants.
options.b: Produce equal quantities at both plants.
options.c: Minimize the lower plant's output regardless of cost.
options.d: Equalize marginal costs across plants.

questions.text: If plant 1 has a lower marginal cost than plant 2 at the current split of a fixed total output, what should the firm do?

options.a: Shift output from plant 1 to plant 2.
options.b: Close plant 1 necessarily.
options.c: Increase production in both plants while holding total output fixed.
options.d: Shift some output from plant 2 to plant 1.

questions.text: How is a multi-plant aggregate marginal cost or supply schedule constructed under conventional conditions?

options.a: Horizontally add the output quantities each plant supplies at a common marginal cost.
options.b: Subtract the higher plant's marginal cost from the lower one's.
options.c: Vertically add the two marginal cost values at fixed output.
options.d: Average all plant costs at identical plant outputs.

questions.text: Why might a firm operate two plants at unequal output levels?

options.a: Total costs cannot depend on plant size.
options.b: Production must be evenly divided by law.
options.c: The two plants can have different marginal cost schedules and equal marginal costs at unequal quantities.
options.d: Equalization of marginal cost requires equal quantities.

questions.text: What distinguishes a long-run cost function from a short-run cost function?

options.a: Long-run costs exclude labor expenses.
options.b: The long run optimizes all inputs, while the short run holds at least one input fixed.
options.c: The long run always has higher cost.
options.d: Short-run costs depend only on market demand.

questions.text: What is the long-run total cost at output y when plant size k can be chosen?

options.a: The maximum of short-run total cost over all plant sizes.
options.b: The minimum of short-run total cost over feasible plant sizes at output y.
options.c: The average of all short-run costs.
options.d: The short-run cost at the smallest plant regardless of output.

questions.text: What is meant by the long-run average cost curve being an envelope?

options.a: It traces the lowest achievable average cost among feasible short-run plant configurations at each output.
options.b: It must always be horizontal.
options.c: It lies above all short-run average cost curves.
options.d: It is the sum of all short-run average cost curves.

questions.text: For a particular plant size optimized for y*, how do SAC and LAC compare at y*?

options.a: LAC must be strictly higher at y*.
options.b: SAC must be strictly lower at y*.
options.c: They coincide at y*.
options.d: Their difference equals price.

questions.text: Can the long-run average cost curve be tangent to a short-run average cost curve away from that short-run curve's minimum?

options.a: Yes, because the plant optimal for a given output need not operate at its own minimum SAC.
options.b: No, short-run and long-run average cost never meet.
options.c: No, tangency only occurs at the minimum SAC.
options.d: Only if fixed costs are negative.

questions.text: When plant size is freely adjustable, why can long-run cost not exceed short-run cost for the same output and particular plant size?

options.a: Long-run output always exceeds short-run output.
options.b: All fixed inputs have zero cost in the long run.
options.c: The long-run choice set includes that short-run plant size among its options.
options.d: Short-run production is always inefficient in its use of variable inputs.

questions.text: With discrete available plant sizes, what can the long-run average cost envelope look like?

options.a: A straight line through every minimum SAC.
options.b: The lower pieces of the corresponding short-run average cost curves, potentially with kinks.
options.c: An upward shift of the highest SAC curve.
options.d: A curve that never touches any SAC curve.

questions.text: What is long-run marginal cost?

options.a: The derivative of fixed cost with respect to output.
options.b: Always the same as average total cost.
options.c: The market price of the fixed input.
options.d: The derivative of optimized long-run total cost with respect to output where it exists.

questions.text: At an output where the optimal short-run plant choice matches the long-run optimum and costs are differentiable, what is generally true?

options.a: Both marginal costs must be zero.
options.b: Short-run marginal cost must exceed long-run marginal cost.
options.c: Short-run and long-run marginal costs coincide.
options.d: Long-run marginal cost is negative.

questions.text: If short-run average cost is tangent to long-run average cost at y*, what does that imply?

options.a: The given plant size is cost minimizing for that output.
options.b: The firm earns zero profit at all prices.
options.c: Output must be at both curves' minima.
options.d: Marginal revenue equals zero.

questions.text: Why is it wrong to infer total fixed cost from the slope of the total cost curve?

options.a: Total cost always has zero slope.
options.b: The slope measures marginal cost, while a fixed-cost term affects the intercept.
options.c: Fixed cost is the derivative of variable cost.
options.d: Fixed costs necessarily rise with output.

questions.text: If the MC curve rises above AVC but stays below AC, which cost behavior is possible?

options.a: AVC must be constant and AC must be rising.
options.b: Both AVC and AC must be falling.
options.c: Both AVC and AC must be rising.
options.d: AVC is rising while AC is still falling.

questions.text: What does an increase in positive fixed costs, holding variable cost fixed, do to the marginal cost curve?

options.a: It makes MC horizontal.
options.b: It lowers MC at every output.
options.c: It shifts MC upward by the fixed cost at every output.
options.d: It leaves MC unchanged.

questions.text: If fixed costs increase while variable costs are unchanged, what happens to average total cost?

options.a: It remains unchanged at every output.
options.b: It increases by the added fixed cost divided by output.
options.c: It becomes identical to marginal cost.
options.d: It necessarily decreases.

questions.text: When marginal cost is constant and fixed cost is positive, what happens to average total cost as output expands?

options.a: It approaches marginal cost from below.
options.b: It equals zero for all output.
options.c: It increases without bound.
options.d: It approaches marginal cost from above.

questions.text: In the cost-curve diagram, why does MC intersect AVC at the minimum of AVC?

options.a: Average variable cost is always below zero there.
options.b: Average variable cost is independent of output.
options.c: Marginal cost equals fixed cost exactly there.
options.d: Marginal cost moves average variable cost down when below it and up when above it.
